title: Slingshot
teaches: The Slingshot as we trade it: a leader that just had a drive pulls back a few closes under the 4-day EMA of the highs, orderly and shallow, and the buy is the first decisive move back over that line, taken as price trades through it and never at the close, never the gap day and never the guess at the low; the stop sits a few cents under the trigger day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

walkthroughs.title: UTHR, September 2025: the textbook Slingshot
steps: UTHR, September 2025. A 37.7% news gap on September 2 is the drive. Then three tiny red days rest under the line.
The line is the 4-day EMA of the highs. Only 9.3% deep, and still above the 50-day and 200-day.
September 18 it pushes back over the line, closing near the high. Buy as it goes through, never at the close.
Stop 402.47, under the day's low. A lower open through it next day says you're wrong. Instead, 3R in 3 sessions.

walkthroughs.title: RELY, November 2024: the earnings-gap Slingshot
steps: Earnings on October 31, 2024 gap RELY up 24.4%, and it closes up 17.8%. That's the drive.
Then a four-day rest: four closes under the line, 7.5% deep. The drive day is never the trigger.
November 20 it pushes back over the line. Buy as it goes through. Stop 19.96, under the day's low.
A weak next day through the stop says no. Instead it climbed steadily along its rising short-term averages, to 13.7R.

walkthroughs.title: URI, November 2016: the trims and the trail
steps: November 9, 2016, the session after the election, URI gaps 9.3% and closes up 17.1%.
Three small red candles under the line. November 21 it pushes back through it. Buy right there, not at the close.
Stop 91.69 under the day's low, 2.3% away. 3R in 6 sessions. Stop to breakeven, first sell into a push.
Sell more into strength, trail the rest on the 9 EMA. The trend ran two months, 17.2R at best.

questions.q: A leader ran hard, then sat three closes under its 4-day EMA of the highs. Today it's pushing back over. What are you looking at?
choices: A Slingshot, the dip snapping back
A breakout over a flat base's top
An Oops reversal, a one-day dip
A gap-up you buy right at the open
questions.answer: A Slingshot, the dip snapping back
questions.why: That's a Slingshot. The stock had its drive, rested a few days under its 4-day EMA of the highs, and now it's snapping back over. A leader that rests shallow and quiet still has its buyers. The buy is the trade back through the line, during the day, not the close. Your stop goes a few cents under that day's low, much tighter than a base breakout's.
questions.lesson_line: A leader rests a few days under the line, then snaps back over. That's the shot.

wrong.A breakout over a flat base's top: A base breakout clears a ceiling after weeks of building. Here it's a few days of rest inside a run, with a much tighter stop.
wrong.An Oops reversal, a one-day dip: An Oops happens inside one session. This one sat under its line for three closes first.
wrong.A gap-up you buy right at the open: A gap is at most the drive that comes before. We never buy the gap day as the Slingshot.

questions.simple: A strong stock rests a few days under its 4-day line, then trades back over it. That's the Slingshot.

reasons: fixed before: choices rewritten for variety 2026-11-10

questions.q: A stock gaps up 18% on earnings and closes over the 4-day EMA of highs that same day. Is that the Slingshot trigger?
choices: No; the gap day is not the trigger
Yes; the close is over the line
Yes, if volume is heavy on the gap
No; the trigger is the first red day
questions.answer: No; the gap day is not the trigger
questions.why: No. The drive day is never the trigger. If the only qualifying drive day is the trigger day itself, it is not a Slingshot. The trigger is the first daily close above the line after a pullback of at least 3 closes under it. An 18% gap or heavy volume does not change that order. Scot1and: take a powerful stock, stretch it with a pullback, then enter when momentum resumes.
questions.lesson_line: The gap is the engine. The Slingshot is the pullback after it, never the gap day itself.

wrong.Yes; the close is over the line: A close over the line on the drive day is the drive, not a trigger. Nothing has pulled back yet.
wrong.Yes, if volume is heavy on the gap: Volume does not turn a gap day into a Slingshot. The order is drive, pullback, then the close back over.
wrong.No; the trigger is the first red day: Buying the first red day of the pullback instead of waiting for the close back over the line is a named mistake. The trigger is the first daily close above the line after the pullback.

questions.simple: No, because the gap day is the drive, and the trigger only comes after a pullback and a close back over the line.

deeper.trap: The gap day looks perfect: a big green bar and a close over the line. That is why it fools people. Before you call anything a trigger, count the closes under the line. With none, there was no pullback, so there is no Slingshot yet.

reasons: settled criterion
fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Your Slingshot stop belongs a few cents under the low of the big drive day.
questions.why: False. The drive day can be days or weeks back, and its low sits way under you. The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day you buy, the trigger day. That's the low of the day, the LOD. If price trades back under it, the snap back failed and you want out. Under the drive day's low you'd risk the whole move, and your size would shrink to almost nothing.
questions.lesson_line: The stop lives under the low of the day you buy. Not the drive day.
questions.simple: False. The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day you buy, not under the drive day.

deeper.trap: Don't mix up the two days. The drive day starts the move. The trigger day is the day price trades back over the line, and its low is the one the stop goes under.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop rule (F62)
fixed before: statement rewritten 2026-11-10

questions.q: A stock sits three closes under its 4-day line in a quiet dip. What has to come before that dip for it to be a Slingshot?
choices: A strong move up, the drive
A long flat base under the highs
A close under the 200-day
A slow volume dry-up to the line
questions.answer: A strong move up, the drive
questions.why: A drive. A Slingshot slings off a strong move up, a big gap or a burst of strong days. The drive tells you buyers just showed up in size. The quiet dip after it says they haven't left. Without the drive there's nothing to sling from, just a stock drifting around a fast line. So find the drive first, then look for the rest.
questions.lesson_line: No drive, no Slingshot.

wrong.A long flat base under the highs: A base is a long rest. The Slingshot wants a fresh burst of strength, then a short dip.
wrong.A close under the 200-day: Closing under the 200-day is a strike against a stock, not a step in this setup.
wrong.A slow volume dry-up to the line: A dry-up describes the dip itself. The drive is the strong move up before it.

questions.simple: A strong move up has to come first. The dip needs something to sling from.

reasons: size of a drive is a held decision (D-106)

questions.q: A Slingshot is only worth your money in a leader: an RS Rating of 80 or more, in a strong group.

We want an RS Rating of 80 or more, a stock outrunning most of the market, in one of the strongest groups. A Slingshot in a laggard is just a bounce. Check the RS Rating before you even draw the line.
questions.lesson_line: A Slingshot in a laggard is just a bounce. Buy the leaders.
questions.simple: True. The setup bets a strong stock keeps going, so it has to be a leader in a strong group.

choices: No, normal volume is fine here
Yes, it needs double the average
Yes, it must beat the dip's volume
No, but it needs light volume

In your head, with a firm exit rule
As a price alert set on the chart

We want the drive and the rest inside an uptrend. Being over the 200-day isn't enough. Look at which way the lines point.
questions.lesson_line: Falling averages mean a downtrend. The Slingshot lives in an uptrend.
questions.simple: False. With the 50-day and 200-day both falling, the stock is in a downtrend, so the pop is just a bounce.

questions.q: The day before the trigger. In Scot1and's words, what lets this Slingshot carry a stop so close to the buy?
choices: The tight range before the trigger
A heavy-volume day on the trigger
A high RS Rating on the stock
A deep pullback that gives it room
questions.answer: The tight range before the trigger
questions.why: The tight range. Scot1and says tight ranges before the trigger show the selling drying up, and more importantly, they permit very tight stops. Here's how. Your stop goes a few cents under the trigger day's low. When the days before it are tight, that low sits right under your buy. UTHR's stop was 1.8%, inside the 1-3% we like.
questions.lesson_line: Tight before the trigger, tight stop after it. That's the edge.

wrong.A heavy-volume day on the trigger: Volume doesn't set the stop. The trigger day's low does.
wrong.A deep pullback that gives it room: The opposite. A deep, loose dip pushes the low away, and the stop with it.
wrong.A high RS Rating on the stock: Strength picks the stock. It doesn't set where the stop sits.

questions.simple: The tight range. It keeps the trigger day's low close to your buy, so the stop is close too.

questions.lesson_line: Liquidity comes before the chart. Under the floor, the shape doesn't matter.

questions.q: Price is pushing back over the 4-day line today. Where do you want it to close by the end of the day?
choices: Near the high of the day
Anywhere, just over the line
Near the low, a shakeout
Right in the middle of the bar
questions.answer: Near the high of the day
questions.why: Near the high. You bought as it went through the line. A close near the high says buyers held it all day and the drive is back on. Our best trigger days closed at 78% to 99% of the day's range. A close in the middle of the bar is a shrug. A close near the low means the push failed, and your stop under the low of the day gets tested fast.
questions.lesson_line: Through the line, then a close near the high. That's a trigger that means it.

wrong.Anywhere, just over the line: Over the line is step one. Where it closes in the day's range tells you if it meant it.
wrong.Near the low, a shakeout: A close near the low is the push failing. Your stop is right under it.
wrong.Right in the middle of the bar: The middle of the bar is a shrug, not the drive starting up again. It's a weaker trigger.

questions.simple: Near the high. That says buyers held it all day and the move is back on.

deeper.example: Our best trigger days closed at 78% to 99% of their range, right near the high of the bar. A mid-bar close is the weaker picture.

On a 3% gap the stock never traded through the line in front of you. In our examples the gap triggers graded lower, B-. A lower grade means a smaller size.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet open, then through the line. A gap trigger is a lower grade.
questions.simple: False. A gap open skips the turn through the line, so it grades lower and gets a smaller size.

questions.q: Four Slingshot pullbacks under the 4-day line. Which one looks like the orderly rest you'd want to buy out of?

One big 5% red bar on volume
A wide 3 ATR swing, two gaps
Any dip, as long as it's 3 closes

questions.simple: Small red bars in a tight range. The stock is resting, not being sold.

wrong.No, wait for a gap up on volume: No surge is needed, and a gap trigger is a lower grade. The trigger is the trade back over the line.

questions.story: The drive was a strong day on big volume. Day one of the pullback is a small red bar closing under the 4-day line. You can feel it coming.
questions.simple: No. The first red day starts the dip, and you buy when price trades back over the line.

deeper.trap: Buying the first red day is a guess at the low. We buy the turn instead, the first trade back over the line. By then the drive is starting up again.

reasons: settled named mistake
four facts agree

questions.q: What do you do with the rest?
choices: Hold, the trail decides
Sell, two months is long enough
Sell on its first red day
Hold until it falls to breakeven
questions.why: Hold. What's left rides the trail, the 9 EMA for a fast mover or the 20 EMA for a steady one like this. You sell on a close below it, and it's still above. Two months is a calendar, not a signal. We swing trade, but a winner can be held as long as it keeps working. GRMN was 50% higher in two months. Trades like that pay for all the small losses.
questions.lesson_line: Part banked, the rest on the trail. Time alone isn't a reason to sell.

wrong.Sell, two months is long enough: A winner can be held as long as it keeps working. The trail decides, not the calendar.
wrong.Sell on its first red day: A red day above the trail isn't an exit. A close below the trail is.
wrong.Hold until it falls to breakeven: Breakeven is a floor for the stop, not the exit for a runner. The trail is.

questions.story: You bought at 66.08, stop 64.04, and sold some on the way up. Two months later it's 50% higher and still above its trail.
questions.simple: Hold. The rest is sold on a close under its trail, not after a set amount of time.

deeper.example: GRMN, trigger 2007-06-11: a five-close rest in a rising leader, bought at 66.08 with the stop at 64.04. It was the steadiest trend of the ten examples, 50% higher in two months. A trend like that is the case for holding while it keeps working.

reasons: rests on rulebook E52 and C35
fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: You find Chris Moody's two-average SlingShot System online. That's the same Slingshot we trade.
questions.why: False. Same name, different setup. Ours is one line, a 4-day EMA of the daily highs. Moody's system uses two averages, and Deepvue describes a 5-day EMA. Run the wrong one and you'll get signals on days we wouldn't touch. Before you trust anything called a Slingshot, check the line.
questions.lesson_line: Same name, different line. Ours is the 4-day EMA of the highs.
questions.simple: False. Ours is one line built from the daily highs, and Moody's uses two averages.

deeper.trap: Same name, different line. Before you trust a signal with this name, check what it draws. Ours is the 4-day EMA of the daily highs.

reasons: held decision D-014 on the line
Deepvue's 5-day dissent

questions.q: Tomorrow morning price trades back over the line. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it, the rest is done
Pass, the gap day was the trigger
Pass, three closes is too long
Take it, a gap this big is the buy
questions.answer: Take it, the rest is done
questions.why: Take it. The news gap was the drive. Then three quiet closes just under the line, tight and orderly. Now price trades back through it. That's your buy, at market as it goes, with the stop a few cents under the low of the day. In our study, filled at the close, UTHR's stop was 1.8% and it hit 3R in 3 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Drive, a quiet rest under the line, then the break back over it.

wrong.Pass, the gap day was the trigger: The gap day is the drive, never the trigger. The trigger is the trade back over the line after the rest.
wrong.Pass, three closes is too long: Three closes under the line is the minimum, not too long.
wrong.Take it, a gap this big is the buy: Right call, wrong reason. The gap is the drive. You buy the trade back over the line after the rest.

questions.simple: Take it. Gap, quiet rest, then the trade back over the line is the whole setup.

deeper.example: UTHR, trigger 2025-09-18: a 37.7% news gap on 2025-09-02 was the drive. Three quiet closes hugged the line, 9.3% deep. Our study bought the close and saw 3R in 3 sessions. A buy through the trigger would differ a little.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's proposed 0.7 line
asks 'take the close' (D-003)

questions.story: A big news gap came first. Then three quiet closes just under the 4-day line.

questions.q: The first day it closes back over its 4-day line after a pullback. Take the close or pass?
choices: Pass; the close sits mid-range
Take it; the close is over the line
Take it; the pullback was short
Pass; wait for heavy volume first
questions.why: Pass. The first close back over the line landed at 0.54 of its range, the middle of the bar. A decisive trigger closes at 0.7 or more, the top 30% of its range. That trade stopped at 0R. It is one case: the card, not the outcome, is the reason.
questions.lesson_line: Look at where the trigger day closed in its own range before you look at the line.

wrong.Take it; the close is over the line: Over the line is the first test. A mid-range close fails the second.
wrong.Take it; the pullback was short: The pullback is fine. The trigger day is the problem.
wrong.Pass; wait for heavy volume first: No volume surge is needed on a trigger day. Ordinary volume is the picture. The close location is the problem.

questions.simple: Pass, because the close landed in the middle of the day's range, at 0.54, and our trigger needs 0.7 or more.

deeper.counter: Compare GSK, a 0.54 close that stopped at 0R, with UTHR, a 0.92 close that reached 3R in 3 sessions. Both were a first close back over the line. One difference you can see on the day is where the close landed.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's proposed 0.7 line
asks 'take the close' (D-003)

questions.q: You've been stopped out of the same stock's Slingshot three times this week. A fourth try has to wait.
questions.why: True. We take at most 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. Three stops in a week means the stock keeps saying no. Each try looked fine on its own, and that's exactly why you need the cap. Without it you can bleed a pile of small losses into one name. Move on, and come back next week if it sets up again.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month. After that the stock has told you something.
questions.simple: True. Three tries in a week is the cap on one stock, and after that it has told you something.

deeper.trap: Each try looks like a fresh setup, so the cap is easy to forget. Count your tries on the stock before you buy.

reasons: rests on rulebook E56

questions.q: What's the right move here?
choices: Sell it before the report
Hold, the trend is up
Sell half, hold the rest
Hold, the stop covers a gap
questions.why: Sell it before the report. We only hold through earnings when the trade is up 5R, and you're at 1.5R. A report can gap the stock right through your stop. A stop can't stop a gap. At 5R you've got the cushion to take that hit. At 1.5R you don't. Book it and look again after the report.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you can't stop. Up 5R buys the ticket, 1.5R doesn't.

wrong.Hold, the trend is up: The trend isn't the test. We hold through a report only at 5R, and this is 1.5R.
wrong.Sell half, hold the rest: The other half still sits through the report at 1.5R. That needs 5R.
wrong.Hold, the stop covers a gap: A stop doesn't cover a gap. Price can open right through it, and the gap rule's 2R ceiling is all you have.

questions.story: Your rally Slingshot is up 1.5R. The report comes out after the close in two sessions.
questions.simple: Sell. It's not up enough to carry through a report, and a stop can't stop a gap.

deeper.trap: Up 1.5R feels like a cushion. It isn't, against a report gap. Even the gap rule has a ceiling: past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you get out.

reasons: rests on rulebook B22
fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: You're in at 13.94, stop 13.42. Seven sessions later it trades 15.50. How many R are you up?
questions.why: 3R. Your risk is 13.94 minus 13.42, 0.52 a share. That's one R. Your gain is 15.50 minus 13.94, 1.56. And 1.56 over 0.52 is 3. Counting in R tells you how the trade is doing against what you risked. It's also where your stop decisions live: somewhere from 2R to 5R it can come up to breakeven. 3R is a mark to judge by, not a sell order.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars.
questions.simple: Divide the gain per share by the risk per share. That's how many R you're up.

deeper.trap: Judging a gain by its percent. The same percent is more R when the stop is close and fewer R when it's wide. We measure every trade in R.

reasons: computed key
the 3R trim is the owner's rule (B19)

wrong.4.0R: Measured the gain from the stop, not from your buy.
wrong.1.6R: Used the dollar gain as R and skipped the divide.
wrong.0.1R: Divided the gain by the price, not by one R.

questions.story: A news gap, a drift back toward the 50-day, then a trigger day that closed near its high.

questions.q: Which grades higher?
choices: The rising 50-day above the 200
Equal; the line is what matters
The flat one; it is less stretched
The one under the 200; more upside
questions.why: The one over a rising 50-day that sits above the 200-day. Our card prefers that location and prefers to avoid a 50-day under the 200-day. The grade then sets the size: A and B setups at normal size, A+ sized up, B- or lower sized down.
questions.lesson_line: Same shape, two locations. Rising averages in the right order earn the better grade.

wrong.Equal; the line is what matters: The line is the trigger. Location grades the trade, and the grade sets the size.
wrong.The flat one; it is less stretched: Less stretched is not a grade. A 50-day under the 200-day is the location we prefer to avoid.
wrong.The one under the 200; more upside: Cheaper is not stronger. Our card prefers a rising 50-day over the 200-day, and prefers to avoid the reverse.

questions.story: Two Slingshots with the same drive and the same tidy pullback. One sits over a rising 50-day above the 200-day. The other sits over a flat 50-day that is under the 200-day.
questions.simple: The Slingshot over a rising 50-day above the 200-day grades higher, because that is the location our card prefers.

deeper.trap: The line is only the trigger. Two charts can share the same line and sit in very different places, and the place moves the grade, not the entry rule. LOW had its 50-day under its 200-day and was stopped on day 1.

reasons: rests on one card line (c12)
preference is a held decision (D-009)
fixed before: lesson line reworded

questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Sell, it's under 1R at 10 days
Hold, the stop hasn't been hit
Add, it's still above the line
Sell half and hold the rest
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold, and this one's at 0.6R. A Slingshot should work fast, the drive starting up again. Ten days of sideways says it didn't. Your money is tied up in a stock doing nothing while better setups go by. The stop is one exit. Time is the other.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.

wrong.Sell half and hold the rest: The time stop sells the trade, not part of it.
wrong.Hold, the stop hasn't been hit: The stop is one exit. The time stop is another, and it just fired.
wrong.Add, it's still above the line: A trade that's done nothing in 10 days isn't asking for more money. The time stop sells it.

questions.story: Ten trading days after a Slingshot buy, the trade sits at 0.6R, drifting sideways. The stop hasn't been touched.
questions.simple: Sell. Under 1R after 10 trading days, the money is better off in a trade that's working.

deeper.trap: Waiting because the stop hasn't hit. Not being stopped out doesn't mean the trade is working.

reasons: a number in the owner's rulebook (C33)
rests on a rule that can change

questions.q: In our Slingshot examples, three of the four losers were stopped out within two sessions of the buy.
questions.why: True. SRPT and LOW were out on day 1, PSX on day 2. PLTR lasted to day 4, then gapped under the stop. That's the design working. When the trigger day's low doesn't hold, the snap back failed, and the stop gets you out small and fast. Four losses is a tiny sample, so don't read a win rate into it. Read the shape: these fail fast, and that keeps them cheap.
questions.lesson_line: A Slingshot that fails, fails fast. The tight stop makes that cheap.
questions.simple: True. When a Slingshot fails, the trigger day's low breaks fast, and the stop gets you out small.

deeper.trap: Four losses is a tiny sample. It shows how these failures looked, not how often a Slingshot fails. What it shows is the design: a stop under the trigger day's low gets you out fast.

reasons: one fact carries it, our own bars dossier
examples not yet reviewed by the owner

questions.q: How do you grade it?
choices: Too sloppy, I'd pass
An A, it's close enough
A B, buy half size
Orderly, it's under 2 ATR
questions.why: Pass. That dip swung 1.85 ATR, nearly two days' worth of the stock's average daily range, and it chopped around the whole way. Our best Slingshots rested quietly, small red bars in a tight range. There's no magic number here. It's how it looks, a rest or a stock getting pushed around. This one's getting pushed around. A loose dip also drags the low away from your buy, so your stop gets wide. I'd let TCOM go.
questions.lesson_line: A big drive doesn't excuse a messy dip.

wrong.An A, it's close enough: A sloppy dip isn't an A. The tight rest is what makes this setup work.
wrong.A B, buy half size: Half of a sloppy setup is still sloppy. I'd pass.
wrong.Orderly, it's under 2 ATR: Under 2 isn't the test. Look at the bars. It chopped up and down the whole way, and that's no rest.

questions.story: The day before it trades back over its line. The whole pullback spans 1.85 ATR, and it's been choppy.
questions.simple: Pass. The dip is wide and choppy, not the quiet rest we want to buy out of.

deeper.trap: A huge drive makes people forgive a messy dip. Look at the rest on its own: a tight range and small red bars. Then look at the drive.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's proposed 1.6 ATR and 3.5%
card lists choppy as both a gate and a B- row
fixed before

questions.q: How big do you go?
choices: Sized down
Normal size
Sized up
No trade
questions.why: Sized down. The grade is your read on how clean the setup is, and the grade sets the size. A and B get normal size, A+ gets sized up, and B- or lower gets sized down, 0.25% to 0.5% risk. Green means full risk for each grade. It doesn't turn a B- into an A. Save the big size for the ones that make you sit up.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the size. Green doesn't upgrade a B-.

wrong.Normal size: Normal size is for A and B setups. A B- gets sized down.
wrong.Sized up: Sizing up is for the A+ only.
wrong.No trade: A B- isn't a skip. It's sized down, to 0.25% to 0.5% risk.

questions.story: Everything checks out, but you'd grade this Slingshot a B-, not one of the clean ones. Our market filter is Green.
questions.simple: Smaller. The grade sets the size, and Green doesn't make a B- any better.

deeper.trap: Green reads like permission to press. It only means full risk per grade. A B- stays a B- in a Green market.

reasons: rests on the owner's grade and risk rules (D38, E49)
sizing by grade is a held decision (D-005)
fixed before: story corrected

questions.q: Tomorrow it trades back over the line and you buy at market. Where's the stop, and when's the first sell?
choices: Under the day's low, day 3 or later
Far under the base, all out at 2R
At the gap's low, and hold it all to 5R
Under the day's low, all out at 3R
questions.answer: Under the day's low, day 3 or later
questions.why: Under the low of the day, and the first sell waits. The stop goes a few cents under the trigger day's low, the low of the day, or LOD. If that low breaks, the snap back failed and you're out small. We very rarely sell on day 1, and day 3 is the earliest we look. Then you sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, by judgment, and trail the rest. URI's stop was 2.3%, and it hit 3R in 6 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Write the plan before the trigger. Stop, first sell, trail.

wrong.Far under the base, all out at 2R: That stop is far too wide, and selling it all at 2R throws away the runner.
wrong.At the gap's low, and hold it all to 5R: The gap low is way under you. The stop goes under the low of the day.
wrong.Under the day's low, all out at 3R: Right stop, wrong exit. The first sell is a judgment, and all out at 3R gives up the trail.

questions.story: A 9.3% gap came first, then three closes under the 4-day line.
questions.simple: Stop under the low of the day. The first sell waits for a push, day 3 or later.

deeper.trap: Write the whole plan before the trigger: entry, stop, first sell, trail. The distance to the stop sets your size. Then carry it out without a debate.

reasons: held decision D-003 (trigger order)
rests on rulebook E51, E57 and F62

questions.q: If it closes back over the line tomorrow, is that a Slingshot?
choices: No, there's no drive to sling from
Yes, the shape is all you need
Yes, a close over the line is enough
No, four closes is too few
questions.answer: No, there's no drive to sling from
questions.why: No. There's nothing to sling from. The setup is a strong move, a short rest, then the move starting up again. This stock just climbed steadily with no drive. The dip and the line are there, the reason isn't. It did reach 4.1R, but there's no telling if that was the setup or just the climb. I want the drive before I call it a Slingshot.
questions.lesson_line: The shape without the drive is just a dip.

wrong.Yes, the shape is all you need: The shape alone isn't the setup. The drive comes first, and it's missing.
wrong.Yes, a close over the line is enough: A close over the line is only the trigger. The drive has to come first.
wrong.No, four closes is too few: Three closes is the minimum, and this has four. The missing piece is the drive.

questions.story: It has closed under its 4-day line four times. In the 25 sessions before the dip: no 5% gap, no 4% day on above-average volume, no 20% gain in five sessions.
questions.simple: No. A strong move up has to come before the dip, and this stock never had one.

deeper.trap: Calling it a Slingshot because the shape looks right. The line and the closes are there. With no drive first, there's nothing to sling from.

reasons: rests on the drive-first line of our card (c44)
story has no strong move under any option of the held drive decision (D-106)

questions.q: Your Slingshot stop only moves down on a gap through it, when the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop.
questions.why: True. Your stop only moves up. The one exception isn't your choice. When the stock gaps through your stop, the first 30 minutes decide. The low of that first bar is the new stop. If those 30 minutes take you past 2R of loss, you get out. The gap made the call, not you. Never stretch this to excuse an ordinary dip through your stop.
questions.lesson_line: One exception, and it isn't yours to choose. The gap decides.
questions.simple: True. The stop only moves up, except on a gap through it, where the first 30-minute low becomes the stop.

deeper.trap: Widening a stop by hand is a mistake we name. The gap rule is different. It replaces a stop the market already went through with a defined one, and it still has a ceiling.

reasons: rests on rulebook A4 and B20

questions.q: What do you buy today?
choices: Nothing today, no setup
The near miss, it's Green
Buy it small, tight stop
A weaker name that fires
questions.why: Nothing today. No setup, no trade, and cash is a position. The near one closed mid-range, so its trigger wasn't decisive, and a near miss is still a miss. Green sets the risk for a setup that passes. It doesn't create one. The days you sit on your hands are part of the job. Never force a trade just to have something on.
questions.lesson_line: Green is permission, not an order. Wait for the one that passes.

wrong.Buy it small, tight stop: Small is a size, not a setup. Don't force a trade to have something on.
wrong.The near miss, it's Green: Green sets the size for a setup that passes. It doesn't create one.
wrong.A weaker name that fires: We buy leaders. A weaker name that fires is still forcing a trade.

questions.story: Earnings season, and our market filter is Green. Nothing on your Slingshot list passes every check. One is close, but its trigger closed mid-range.
questions.simple: Nothing. No setup, no trade, and Green only sets the size for setups that pass.

deeper.trap: A Green market feels like an order to act. It only sets the risk for setups that pass.

reasons: rests on the owner's no-setup rule (D44)
fixed before: choice reworded

questions.q: You bought the trigger close at 66.08 with the stop at 64.04. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 76.28. One R is the fill minus the stop, 66.08 minus 64.04. Add five of those to the fill to get 5R. The second third comes off there, and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 5R before the open. The second third comes off there.
questions.simple: One R is the buy price minus the stop, so 5R is the buy price plus five times that gap.

reasons: computed key
the 5R trim is the owner's rule (E51)

questions.q: How many shares ride the trail?
choices: 30 shares, on the trail
60 shares, on the trail
45 shares, on the trail
15 shares, on the trail
questions.why: 30 shares. You bought 90, sold 30 into the first push and 30 more into this one. 90 minus 30 minus 30 leaves 30. Both sells were judgment calls, into strength. The last 30 is your runner. It rides the 9 EMA if it's a fast mover, the 20 EMA if it's steadier, and goes on a close below.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into pushes by judgment. What's left trails.

wrong.60 shares, on the trail: That's what was left after the first sell. You sold 30 more today.
wrong.45 shares, on the trail: Half of 90 is 45, but two sells of 30 leave 30.
wrong.15 shares, on the trail: That takes another 15 off. Two sells of 30 leave 30.

questions.story: You bought 90 shares of a Slingshot at the trigger. You sold 30 into a push. Today it pushes again and you sell 30 more.
questions.simple: Two sells of 30 out of 90 leave 30 shares, and those ride the trail.

reasons: rests on rulebook E51, adjustable

questions.story: A stock traded flat for three months, no gap, no big up day. It then closed under its 4-day EMA of the highs four days running. Today it surges on heavy volume and closes back over the line near its high.
questions.q: Is today the Slingshot buy?
choices: No, the drive can't be the trigger
Yes, four closes under, then over
Yes, heavy volume makes it a drive
No, it needs a gap open to count
questions.answer: No, the drive can't be the trigger

wrong.Yes, four closes under, then over: That's only the dip and the move back over. No drive came before it.
wrong.Yes, heavy volume makes it a drive: Even if today is a drive day, the drive day is never the trigger.
wrong.No, it needs a gap open to count: A gap open isn't what's missing, and a gap trigger grades lower anyway. The drive before the dip is missing.

questions.why: No. The drive has to come before the dip, and three flat months gave it nothing to sling from. Today's surge might be the start of a drive. But the drive day is never the trigger. If it keeps going, watch for a short rest under the line after it. That's when you've got a real Slingshot.
questions.lesson_line: A big day after a dip isn't the drive. The drive comes before the rest.
questions.simple: No. The drive comes first, then the rest, then the trigger, and today can't be two of those.

reasons: settled criterion
no strength before the pullback, so the key holds under every D-106 option

questions.q: Your Slingshot buy point was 40.00. You were away, and now it's 42.20. Do you buy?
choices: No, it's 5.5% over the buy point
Yes, it's only 2.2% over the buy point
Yes, with a wider stop to fit
Yes, but at half size
questions.answer: No, it's 5.5% over the buy point
questions.why: No. 42.20 minus 40.00 is 2.20, and 2.20 over 40.00 is 5.5%. We never buy more than 4% over the buy point. That's chasing. Your stop still sits under the buy point. So the higher you pay, the wider the stop and the fewer shares you get. You pay more for less. I'd rather miss it than chase it.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the buy point and I'm done.

wrong.Yes, with a wider stop to fit: We don't widen a stop to fit a late buy. Past 4% we pass.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Half size doesn't fix a late buy. It's past 4% over the buy point.
wrong.Yes, it's only 2.2% over the buy point: That reads the 2.20 dollars as a percent. As a percent of 40.00 it's 5.5%.

questions.simple: No. It's 5.5% over the buy point, past our limit, so buying now is chasing.

reasons: a number in the owner's rulebook (C28)
